title: Does adoption spread through village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed?
summary: Research programme on the 43 Karnataka village networks of Banerjee, Chandrasekhar, Duflo and Jackson (2013; CC0 replication data, 9,126 households, 44,367 ties): can cross-sectional adoption data tell a simple contagion from a complex one, and which seeding rule stays near the best under every model the data cannot reject? Milestone 1 ports the authors’ estimation code (information model, five moments, identity weights, their 31 × 39 grid, Bayesian bootstrap). It reproduces the data (non-leader take-up 18.7% vs 18.5% published, leaders 24.7% vs 24.8%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98.4% of 1,000 bootstrap draws) and the counterfactual (take-up falls by 0.337 with non-adopters silent; paper 0.32), but not the published point: the minimum is q<sub>N</sub> = 0.05, q<sub>P</sub> = 0.30 for three seeds against 0.10, 0.50, which scores 11 times our minimum; q<sub>P</sub> is weakly identified (95% interval 0.15–1.0) and moves to 0.15–0.25 with two-step weights or quarterly periods. Milestone 2 fits two complex-contagion models on the same information spread, a reinforcement model (logit gains γ per adopting neighbour) and a fractional threshold, and compares them leaving one village out. Both fit better in sample (reinforcement γ = 0.10, positive in 99.5% of 1,000 bootstrap draws, criterion 41% lower; this fine-grid, free-intercept fit is post hoc, the pre-registered coarse grid gave γ = 0) yet predict held-out villages worse than the simple model (better in 13 and 19 of 43; in 12% and 24% of paired bootstrap draws). Take-up by adopting neighbours, 8.3% with none to 35.0% with four or more, is more convex than the simple model's 8.1% to 27.2%, a shape reinforcement, homophily or degree could each leave. Milestone 3 simulates 200 datasets from each fitted model on the real networks and refits all three: in sample the criterion picks the reinforcement model for 85% of datasets the simple model made; leaving one village out recovers the true model 58.5%, 82% and 55.5% of the time (simple, threshold, reinforcement), so milestone 2’s verdict is weak evidence. The moment map’s weakest direction trades the base adoption rate against word of mouth and reinforcement (condition number 79). A post-hoc check finds the real villages’ held-out errors two to four times larger than any model produces in its own synthetic data: every model is too homogeneous across villages. Village heterogeneity and seeding come next.
lede: research programme: does adoption spread through real village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed? On the 43 Banerjee et al. (2013) microfinance villages, simulation shows the estimation recovers the true contagion model only 55 to 82% of the time out of sample (in sample it almost always picks the biggest model), and the real villages differ from each other two to four times more than any fitted model allows.
